prime.problem: Reduction needs a cheap, model-independent reason to keep a test. "It runs code nothing else runs" is the classic one, but running code isn't checking it, so a suite reduced by coverage alone can lose the tests that actually catch bugs.
prime.fits: Test-suite reduction merges three requirements. Mutation testing was the stricter theoretical one; this is the weakest, and the worked example reuses the same is_prime tests and mutants.
expect: a test's requirement = the branches it hits
prime.goal: Compute which branches each test hits, reduce by coverage alone, and show a seeded bug that the 100%-coverage subset misses.

attend: Why do the taken and not-taken outcomes of one if count as two separate requirements?
In the worked example, why is T2 (n = 2) dropped by coverage but essential for catching M1?
Why does 100% branch coverage leave GPT-4 at 86.0, so close to base HumanEval's 88.4?
Why is branch coverage preferred over line coverage and over path coverage here?
If coverage is the weakest requirement, what does the paper say it still guarantees?

must: Requirement = branches a test executes → a test that repeats already-covered branches adds nothing → reduction drops it → even if it is the only input on a boundary a bug moves (n = 2 for M1)

Coverage measures execution, not checking → a subset can hit 6/6 branches and still miss a seeded bug → coverage-only reduction keeps few catching tests → GPT-4 stays at 86.0 vs 76.2 on full HumanEval+

Both outcomes of every decision, nothing more → finite and cheap to measure (unlike paths, which multiply with loop counts) → stricter than lines (an if without else) → a standard, model-independent floor for reduction
elevated: In is_prime, n = 2 makes range(2, 2) empty → reaches return True without entering the loop → the only test on the M1 boundary shares all its branches with others → coverage can't tell it matters

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3 sentences what branch coverage measures, how it becomes a reduction requirement, and why a 100%-coverage subset can still miss a bug. Use the n = 2 case.
checklist: counts both outcomes of every decision executed by the tests
a test's requirement set is its branches; greedy keeps a covering subset
executing a branch isn't checking its result
n = 2 covers nothing new, so it's dropped, but it's the only input killing M1
table 4: coverage alone is the most lenient (86.0)

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between "this test executes the branch" and "this test would notice a bug in the branch", using M1.
answer: T1, T3 and T4 execute both outcomes of that condition
only n = 2 sits where the two conditions differ

retrieve.q: Walk the greedy coverage reduction: which test is picked first and why, and why is T2 then worth 0?
answer: T4 (n = 7) hits b2, b3, b4, b6: 4 new, picked first
T3 adds b5; T1 adds b1
T2 hits only b2 and b4, both already covered: 0 new

retrieve.q: If coverage is so lenient, why not drop it and reduce by mutants and sample kills only?
answer: it guarantees every branch is still exercised
the paper keeps it and mutation as base guarantees for theoretical test adequacy
sample kills alone depend on which models were in the pool

compare.q: On the same four tests, coverage keeps {T4, T3, T1} and mutation keeps {T2, T3, T4}. What does each drop, why, and which dropped test would you miss more?
answer: coverage drops T2 (no new branch) and so loses M1
mutation drops T1 (kills nothing) and so loses branch b1
missing T2 lets a real boundary bug through; missing T1 only leaves one branch unexercised

compare.q: Reduction guarantees every requirement is still met. With coverage as the only requirement, what exactly is guaranteed, and why isn't that enough?
answer: every branch the full suite hit is still hit
nothing guarantees the results on those branches are checked
so tests that caught wrong outputs can be dropped, and scores rise toward base HumanEval

predict.q: Add a fifth test, T5 with n = 9, to the four. Commit: which branches does it hit, would coverage-only greedy ever pick it, and which of M1–M4 does it kill?
predict.answer: n = 9 hits b2, b3, b6 (i = 2 doesn't divide) and b5 (i = 3 divides): 4 branches, tied with T4 in round 1, so greedy may pick it first. It kills none of M1–M4: M1 and M4 differ only at n = 2 or on primes, M2 still finds the divisor 3, and M3 returns False at i = 2, which happens to be the right answer for 9. Coverage greed can prefer a test that detects nothing.

apply.task: Check the prediction in Python: for n in {1, 2, 4, 7, 9}, record the branches hit (instrument the function with a set you add labels to) and which of M1–M4 each input kills. Then run coverage-only greedy with T5 included, breaking the round-1 tie in favour of T5, and report the kept tests and how many mutants they kill.
apply.done: T5 hits {b2, b3, b5, b6} and kills no mutant. Greedy with T5 first keeps T5, then T4 (adds b4) and T1 (adds b1): 3 tests, 6/6 branches, and they kill M3 and M4 only (2/4); M1 and M2 survive.
apply.hint: After T5 = {b2, b3, b5, b6}, T4 adds only b4, T2 adds only b4, T1 adds only b1, T3 adds nothing. Ties again: break toward T4.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: T5's branches, or that it kills none of the mutants?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the paper keeps coverage despite its 86.0?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: branch executed → test kept, or test kept → bug caught?
Could you explain why path coverage is impractical for a loop over range(2, n)?
What will you look for in the sampling-temperature card: how the samples being judged were produced?
